title: Inverse-Designed Nanobeam Cavities for High-Cooperativity Spin-Photon Interfaces in Silicon
authors: Nail Letty, Md Sakibul Islam, Wayesh Qarony
abstract: Telecom-band spin defects in silicon offer a compelling platform for integrated quantum networks by combining scalable silicon photonics with spin-based quantum memories and multiqubit registers. The T center and recently demonstrated Al1 center are particularly promising, but their limited coherent zero-phonon emission requires strong cavity enhancement for efficient spin-photon interfaces. Here, we inverse-design silicon nanobeam cavities for both centers using a unified adjoint-optimization framework targeting Purcell enhancement, resonance alignment, and photon extraction. For each emitter, symmetric cavities maximize Purcell enhancement, while asymmetric cavities provide directional coupling to an integrated waveguide. Three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulations yield loaded quality factors up to 3.25 x 10^6, Purcell factors up to 1.43 x 10^5, and cooperativities of approximately 280-5000, corresponding to cavity-coupled emission fractions exceeding 99.6%. The asymmetric cavities direct approximately 90% of emitted power into a single on-chip waveguide while maintaining cooperativity above 280. Under nanometer-scale fabrication perturbations, all four designs remain within the high-cooperativity regime, and high cooperativity persists when the cavity quality factor is constrained to a realistic absorption-limited value of 10^5. This unified, fabrication-compatible framework establishes a scalable cavity-design route for silicon telecom spin-photon interfaces and, to our knowledge, the first cavity designs for the Al1 center.
summary: This paper presents an inverse-design methodology to engineer silicon nanobeam cavities optimized for coupling spin defects (T and Al1 centers) to photons. By simultaneously optimizing for Purcell enhancement and directional coupling, the authors achieve high cooperativities necessary for quantum information transfer. This provides a scalable, fabrication-compatible route for integrated quantum photonic devices.
main_problem: The core challenge is creating efficient spin-photon interfaces to transfer quantum information from stationary spin memories to flying photonic qubits for integrated quantum networks.
main_result: The authors successfully designed two complementary cavity geometries—symmetric and asymmetric—that achieve high cooperativities ($\approx 280-5000$) for silicon spin defects like the T and Al1 centers.
method: They employed a unified adjoint-optimization framework within 3D FDTD simulations to simultaneously optimize Purcell enhancement, resonance alignment, and directional photon extraction.
model_or_system: The system involves telecom-band spin defects (T and Al1 centers) embedded in silicon, coupled to engineered silicon nanobeam cavities. The design process optimizes the cavity geometry to maximize the coupling rate ($g$) relative to decoherence rates.
key_observables: Cooperativity ($C$), Purcell Factor ($F_P$), and the fraction of emitted power coupled into the on-chip waveguide ($ eta_R$).
important_parameters: High cooperativity ($C \gg 1$), fabrication-compatible lattice parameters, and the ability to maintain performance under realistic absorption-limited quality factors ($Q \approx 10^5$).
main_assumptions: The optimization is restricted to modifying lattice parameters of a conventional nanobeam structure, ensuring fabrication compatibility.
figures_summary: The figures illustrate the adjoint-optimization pipeline, comparing the operating principles of symmetric (for maximal Purcell enhancement) and asymmetric (for directional coupling) cavity designs.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical need for high-cooperativity interfaces, details the adjoint-optimization methodology for cavity design, presents the results for two complementary cavity types, and confirms the robustness of these designs against fabrication imperfections.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of coupling solid-state quantum emitters to photonic circuits, which is central to building scalable quantum networks and quantum repeaters.
